name: Yorkshire flat cap
desc: Flat caps took over the mill and pit towns of the North because a square of cloth made one cheaply.

name: Donegal tweed cap
desc: Donegal tweed is known for the bright flecks, called neps, spun into the yarn.

name: Luton straw boater
desc: Luton made hats for so long that its football club is still nicknamed the Hatters.

name: Panama hat
desc: Panama hats come from Ecuador, not Panama; the name stuck after workers on the canal wore them.

name: Red bobble hat
desc: Wool traps air in its crimped fibres, so a knitted hat stays warm even when it gets damp.

name: Green bobble hat
desc: The knit-and-purl stitches in a hat make it stretch, which is why one size fits most heads.

name: Bucket hat
desc: The bucket hat became the badge of Manchester's late 1980s and 1990s music scene.

name: Sou'wester
desc: Its long back brim sheds rain off your neck; the name comes from the south-westerly gales.

name: Tam o' shanter
desc: The tam o' shanter is named for the hero of Robert Burns's poem of 1790, who rode home past Alloway Kirk.

name: Deerstalker
desc: The deerstalker has two peaks and flaps to tie up, made for stalking in Scottish weather.

name: Hard hat
desc: A hard hat has a webbing cradle inside, so a blow spreads across the whole head.

name: Headscarf
desc: A silk headscarf was the style of the Queen's country walks and of every 1960s film star.

name: Straw sunhat
desc: Straw plait was made across Bedfordshire and Hertfordshire for centuries, mostly by women and children at home.

name: Fair Isle jumper
desc: Fair Isle knitting comes from a tiny island between Orkney and Shetland and uses no more than two colours in a row.

name: Aran jumper
desc: Aran jumpers are named for the Aran Islands off Galway Bay, and the cables are knitted into thick undyed wool.

name: Guernsey jumper
desc: The guernsey is a tightly knitted wool jumper, traditionally navy, made for fishermen of the Channel Islands.

name: Jersey jumper
desc: Jersey the cloth is named for the island, where knitters made hardwearing woollen jerseys for fishermen.

name: Derry shirt
desc: In the nineteenth century Derry became a great shirt-making city, with factories along the Foyle.

name: Belfast linen shirt
desc: Belfast was nicknamed Linenopolis in the nineteenth century for its linen mills.

name: Three-legs T-shirt
desc: The three legs of Man have been the island's emblem since the thirteenth century.

name: Fisherman's smock
desc: Cornish fishing crews wore loose canvas frocks over their ganseys to keep the spray off.

name: White T-shirt
desc: A T-shirt is named for its shape, and a white one is the quickest way to find out what you have spilled.

name: Navy T-shirt
desc: Navy dye was once made from woad and indigo; this one is made in a laundry-friendly way instead.

name: Grey hoodie
desc: Hooded sweatshirts date from the 1930s, when they were made to keep warehouse workers warm.

name: Green hoodie
desc: Hoodies were first sold in the 1930s as workwear for American cold-store workers.

name: Striped Breton top
desc: The striped Breton top was a French navy uniform, and the stripes made someone overboard easier to spot.

name: Mustard cardigan
desc: A cardigan is named for the seventh Earl of Cardigan, who led the Charge of the Light Brigade.

name: Hooped rugby shirt
desc: Rugby is named for Rugby School in Warwickshire, where the game is said to have begun in 1823.

name: Lab coat
desc: A lab coat is cut long to cover the clothes underneath, which is entirely the point.

name: Harris Tweed jacket
desc: Only cloth handwoven by islanders in their own homes in the Outer Hebrides may carry the Orb mark.

name: Herringbone tweed jacket
desc: Herringbone weave zigzags like the bones of a herring, and it is the commonest tweed pattern.

name: Waxed jacket
desc: A waxed cotton jacket sheds rain because the wax fills the weave; it needs rewaxing every year.

name: Navy waxed jacket
desc: Waxed cotton took over from oilskin for coastal and country wear in the twentieth century.

name: Oilskin coat
desc: Oilskins were once cotton treated with linseed oil, and they smelled exactly as you would imagine.

name: Welsh tapestry coat
desc: Welsh tapestry is a double cloth, so the same pattern appears on the back in opposite colours.

name: Hi-vis vest
desc: Fluorescent yellow-green sits where the human eye is most sensitive, which is why roadworkers wear it.

name: Quilted gilet
desc: Gilet is simply the French word for waistcoat.

name: Striped apron
desc: Blue-and-white stripe is the traditional cloth of the butcher's apron.

name: Dungarees
desc: Dungaree is a coarse cotton cloth, named for a district of Mumbai.

name: Indigo jeans
desc: Denim was woven in Nimes, in France; the word comes from de Nimes.

name: Stone chinos
desc: Chinos got their name from the cotton twill first woven in China for army uniforms.

name: Cord trousers
desc: Corduroy ridges are called wales, and a thick-wale cord is the sound of every university seminar.

name: Khaki shorts
desc: Khaki is the Urdu word for dusty, and the army colour of the same name hid in dry ground.

name: Pleated skirt
desc: A pleated skirt keeps its folds only if you leave it alone, which is why it is a school staple.

name: Tartan skirt
desc: Tartan was banned by law in Scotland after 1746 and legal again in 1782.

name: Black Watch kilt
desc: Black Watch tartan began as the pattern of the Highland companies raised in the 1720s to keep watch on the Highlands.

name: Royal Stewart kilt
desc: Royal Stewart is the sovereign's personal tartan, and anyone is welcome to wear it.

name: Hunting Stewart kilt
desc: A hunting tartan is the muted version of a clan's cloth, meant for the hills rather than the ballroom.

name: Northampton brogues
desc: The holes in a brogue were once there to let water out of boots that crossed Irish and Scottish bogs.

name: Cherry-red boots
desc: Northampton shoemakers have supplied boots to armies since the English Civil War.

name: Red wellies
desc: The Wellington boot is named for the first Duke of Wellington, who asked for a hardier version of the Hessian boot.

name: Green wellies
desc: Rubber wellies were first made in Britain in Edinburgh, at the North British Rubber Company, in the 1850s.

name: Yellow wellies
desc: Bright yellow is the old oilskin colour of the fishing fleets, easy to spot against a grey sea.

name: Navy wellies
desc: Millions of pairs of wellingtons were made for the soldiers of the First World War.

name: Black trainers
desc: Plimsolls got their name because the line round the sole looks like a ship's Plimsoll line.

name: Black school shoes
desc: Leather shoes last longer if you rest them a day between wears, because the leather needs to dry.

name: Hiking boots
desc: The Lake District fells are ground out by boots like these: the Pennine Way alone is 268 miles.

name: Lancashire clogs
desc: Wooden-soled clogs were mill-floor wear in Lancashire, and clog dancing grew from their rhythms.

name: Welsh wool shawl
desc: Newtown in Powys was once called the Leeds of Wales for its flannel mills.

name: Shetland lace shawl
desc: A good Shetland lace shawl is knitted so fine that it can be drawn through a wedding ring.

name: Nottingham lace collar
desc: Nottingham's Lace Market was the centre of English machine-made lace in the nineteenth century.

name: Paisley scarf
desc: The Paisley pattern is named for the Scottish town that wove imitation Kashmir shawls in the nineteenth century.

name: Red football scarf
desc: Supporters wore knitted scarves in team colours from the early twentieth century.

name: Blue football scarf
desc: A football scarf is knitted long enough to hold up at the anthem, and short enough not to trip on.

name: Black and white scarf
desc: Stripes in a scarf come from joining different wool colours as the row changes.

name: Morris sash
desc: Morris dancing was recorded in England by the fifteenth century.

name: Cheshire cheese rosette
desc: Cheshire is one of the oldest named English cheeses, said to appear in the Domesday Book.

name: Conference lanyard
desc: The lanyard is a sailor's word for a cord, and now hangs round the necks of every committee in Britain.

name: Round glasses
desc: Spectacles were invented in Italy in the thirteenth century and reached England soon after.

name: Tortoiseshell glasses
desc: Real tortoiseshell was long ago replaced by plastic, to the great relief of the tortoises.

name: Handlebar moustache
desc: The Handlebar Club of Britain was founded in 1947 and has strict rules about the curl.

name: Festival glitter
desc: Glastonbury began in 1970 at Worthy Farm, and the first ticket included free milk.

name: Black umbrella
desc: Jonas Hanway is said to have been the first Londoner to carry an umbrella daily, in the 1750s.

name: Hurley
desc: Hurling is often called the fastest field game in the world, and its ball is a sliotar.

name: Shinty caman
desc: Shinty is played with a stick called a caman, and is closely related to Irish hurling.

name: Shepherd's staff
desc: A shepherd's crook hooks a sheep by the leg, which is a lot easier than chasing it.

name: Fiddle
desc: Shetland has a famous fiddle tradition, with a style of its own.

name: Hurricane lantern
desc: A hurricane lantern has a glass chimney, so the flame stays lit in a gale.

name: Field notebook
desc: Gilbert White's 1789 Natural History of Selborne grew from a lifetime of notes on one Hampshire village.

name: Red rucksack
desc: A good rucksack carries its weight on the hips, not the shoulders.

name: Bagpipes
desc: The Great Highland bagpipe has three drones and a chanter.

name: Salmon rod
desc: Atlantic salmon return to the river where they hatched, sometimes after thousands of miles at sea.

name: Binoculars
desc: Binoculars marked 8x42 magnify eight times, and let in a lot of light for dusk birds.
